chunks.label: Definition 1.
chunks.text:
Definition 1. A group is the data of a pair (G, f) consisting of a set G together with a function
f : G × G −→G
such that:
(A) For all g1, g2, g3 ∈G,
f (︁g1, f(g2, g3) )︁= f (︁f(g1, g2), g3 )︁.
(Id) There is an e ∈G such that, for every g ∈G,
f(e, g) = f(g, e) = g.
(Inv) For every g ∈G, there is a g′ ∈G such that
f(g, g′) = f(g′, g) = e.
Furthermore, G is said to be abelian, or commutative, if
f(g1, g2) = f(g2, g1)
for all pairs g1, g2 ∈G.

chunks.label: Remark 1.
chunks.text: Remark 1. The labels (A), (Id) and (Inv) stand for associativity, identity and inverse.

chunks.label: Remark 2.
chunks.text: Remark 2. We remark that the element e of condition (Inv) in Definition 1 is the same element e of condition (Id) of loc. cit., which from Proposition 1 is unique.

chunks.label: Proposition 1.
chunks.text: Proposition 1. Consider a set G with a function f : G × G →G which satisfies conditions (A) and (Id) above. Then the element e of condition (Id) is unique.

chunks.label: Proof.
chunks.text:
Proof. Let e1 and e2 be two elements in G satisfying condition (Id). Then
e1 = f(e1, e2) = e2
where the first equality follows from the fact that e1 satisfies property (Id), and the second equality follows from the fact that e2 satisfies property (Id). In particular, e1 = e2.

chunks.label: Notation 1.
chunks.text:
Notation 1. Given a group (G, f) and g1, g2 ∈G, we will use the notation
g1 · g2 := f(g1, g2).
In particular, condition (A) translates into
g1 · (g2 · g3) = (g1 · g2) · g3.
Moreover, we will denote the identity element by 1.

chunks.label: Notation 2.
chunks.text: Notation 2. When writing a group G, we will often omit the operation f. So instead of writing “consider a group (G, f)”, we will often write “consider a group G”, when we believe that there is no ambiguity.

chunks.label: Notation 3.
chunks.text: Notation 3. If G is a commutative group, instead of writing · we will write + for the group operation. So for example instead of writing g1 · g2, we will write g1 + g2. If as above we use the notation + for the operation, we will denote the identity element by 0.

chunks.label: Notation 4.
chunks.text: Notation 4. Given g ∈G, we will denote by g−1 an element of G as in condition (Inv) of Definition 1.

chunks.label: Example 1.
chunks.text:
Example 1. Here are some examples of groups:
1. The additive integers (Z, +) are an abelian group.
2. GLn = {A an n × n matrix : det A̸ = 0}
with matrix multiplication is a non-abelian group.
3. (Q∗, ·) is a multiplicative non-abelian group.
4. Non-example: {n ∈Z : n̸ = 0, ·}.
5. Let X be a non-empty set and
Fun(X) := {f : X →X}.
Equipped with composition. The pair
(Fun(X), composition of functions)
is not a group. If instead we restrict to bijective functions, then it is a group.

chunks.label: Definition 2 (Permutation Group).
chunks.text: Definition 2 (Permutation Group). If X is a set, the set of bijective functions from X to X, equipped with function composition is called the group of permutations of X and is denoted SX. If |X| = n, then we also write Sn.

chunks.label: Definition 3 (Homomorphism of Group).
chunks.text:
Definition 3 (Homomorphism of Group). Let (G1, ·1) and (G2, ·2) be groups. A function f : G1 → G2 is said to be a homomorphism if
f(g1 ·1 g2) = f(g1) ·2 f(g2).

chunks.label: Example 2.

Example 2. 1. The identity function Id: G →G.
2. log: (R+, ·) −→(R, +).
3. det: GLn −→(R \ {0}, ·).

chunks.label: Definition 1.
chunks.text:
Definition 1. Let G1, G2 be groups. We call a map f : (G1, ·1) →(G2, ·2) a homomorphism if
f(g1 ·1 g2) = f(g1) ·2 f(g2) for all g1, g2 ∈G1

chunks.label: Remark 1.
chunks.text:
Remark 1.
(i) Let f : G1 →G2 be a group homomorphism. Let id1, id2 be the identity elements for
G1, G2 respectively. We have that f(id1) = id2. This follows from
f(id1) = f(id1 ·1 id1) = f(id1) ·2 f(id1)
This gives
f(id1) = f(id1) ·2 f(id1)−1 = id2
(ii) For any g ∈G1, we have f(g−1) = f(g)−1. This follows from
id2 = f(id1) = f(g ·1 g−1) = f(g) ·2 f(g−1)
(iii) Let f1 : G1 →G2 and f2 : G2 →G3 are group homomorphisms. Then f2 ◦f1 : G1 →
G3 is also a group homomorphism. (Check as an exercise.)
(iv) if f : G1 →G2 is a bijective group homomorphism, then f−1 is a group homomor-
phism. (Check as an exercise.)

chunks.label: Definition 2.
chunks.text: Definition 2. We call f : G1 →G2 a group isomorphism if it is a bijective homomorphism.

chunks.label: Example 1.
chunks.text: Example 1. Consider the map (R, +) 7→(R>0, ·) defined by the exponential map. This is a group isomorphism as it has an inverse defined by log.

chunks.text:
Definition 3. Let G be a group. A subgroup of G is a subset H ⊆G so that
(i) idG ∈H
(ii) for all a, b ∈H, a · b ∈H
(iii) for a ∈H, a−1 ∈H

chunks.label: Example 2.
chunks.text: Example 2. Take G = GL2 and H1 = {M ∈GL2 : det(M) = 1} and H2 = {id}.

Remark 2. (i) Notice that a subset of a group satisfying conditions (ii), (iii) but not (i) has to be the empty set.
(ii) A non-example of a subgroup would be (Z\{0}, ×) ⊆(Q\{0}, ×). It satisfies conditions
(i), (ii) but not (iii).

chunks.label: Probosition 1.
chunks.text: Probosition 1. Let f : G1 →G2 be a group homomorphism. Then ker(f) ⊆G1 and im(f) ⊆G2 are subgroups.

chunks.label: Proof.
chunks.text:
Proof. (i) ker(f) is a subgroup. Let’s check the axioms. We know that f(id1) = id2 since f is a homomorphism. Hence id1 ∈ker(f). Let a, b ∈ker(f). Then we have
f(a · b) = f(a) · f(b) = id2 · id2 = id2 hence a · b ∈ker(f). Finally, suppose that a ∈ker(f). We have
id2 = f(a) = f(a · a · a−1) = f(a) · f(a) · f(a−1) = id2 · id2 ·f(a−1)
and hence a−1 ∈ker(f).
(ii) Showing that im(f) is a subgroup is left as an exercise.
□

Theorem (Lagrange): Given two groups H < G, then |H| divides |G|, or
|H| | |G|

|a| | |G|
